title: What Is a Mixture of Experts?
hook: Instead of running every input through one big network, route each token to a few specialist sub-networks - total capacity grows without proportional compute.
key_points: A gating network learns which 'expert' sub-networks to activate for each input, typically selecting just 1-2 out of dozens.
Total parameter count scales with the number of experts, but compute per token stays roughly constant.
Experts tend to specialize organically - different ones handle different domains or token types.
Load balancing is a key challenge: poorly tuned gates cause some experts to be over-used and others ignored.
content_html: Mixture of Experts (MoE) is an architecture pattern where a model contains many parallel sub-networks ("experts") and a learned gate that selects only a small subset to process each input. Shazeer and colleagues formalized this for deep learning in a 2017 paper on sparsely-gated MoE for language modeling.
extra_html:
How it works

A gating function (usually a small linear layer with a softmax or top-k operation) scores each expert for the current input and routes the token to the top-k scorers - often just 1 or 2. Each expert is a feed-forward network. The outputs of the chosen experts are weighted and summed. Because only a fraction of experts activate per token, the total floating-point operations stay low even as total parameters grow into the billions or trillions.

Why it matters

MoE is the architecture behind some of the largest and most compute-efficient models in production today, including Mixtral and the Switch Transformer. It lets teams scale model capacity without proportionally scaling training or inference cost - a significant lever when hardware is the bottleneck. The original 2017 paper on arXiv is a good starting point for the formal treatment.

related.title: Switch Transformer: Scaling to Trillion-Parameter Models
related.hook: Route every token to exactly one expert instead of many - this single simplification made trillion-parameter MoE models stable enough to train at scale.

related.title: Mixtral of Experts
related.hook: Mixtral packs 8 experts per layer but routes each token through only 2, so you get the capacity of a ~47B model at the compute cost of a ~13B one - open weights included.

related.title: Attention Is All You Need
related.hook: Drop recurrence and convolution, keep only attention — and you get a model that trains in parallel and powers nearly every LLM since.

related.title: Redesigning MoE Routers with Manifold Power Iteration
related.hook: An MoE router points each token at the right expert — yet nothing forces its rows to actually represent those experts. This aligns each router row with its expert's principal direction.

flashcards.prompt: How does MoE grow total capacity without growing compute per token?
flashcards.back_html: A gating network activates only a small subset of experts (often 1-2 of dozens) per input, so total parameters scale with experts but per-token FLOPs stay roughly constant.

flashcards.prompt: What is a key challenge in training a Mixture of Experts?

choices.text: Load balancing — poorly tuned gates over-use some experts and ignore others
Experts must all be trained on the same identical data
The gate requires a separate dataset of expert labels

flashcards.explanation_html: Load balancing is highlighted as a key challenge: bad gates cause uneven expert usage.

flashcards.prompt: What does the gating network do in an MoE layer?
flashcards.back_html: It scores each expert for the input and routes the token to the top-k scorers; their outputs are then weighted and summed.
